Today we're launching Perplexity Frontier Research.

The goal of Perplexity Frontier Research is to create a system that can perform autonomous research.

The work will focus on multi-agent orchestration, reinforcement learning, continual learning, systems, and pre-training.

We will develop algorithms, models, and evaluations, released openly, and tested in Perplexity products. Our work will be supported by more than 10,000 GPUs.

The Frontier Research team will regularly publish papers, models, data, and benchmarks.

We're actively hiring researchers and engineers for Perplexity Frontier Research in San Francisco, Palo Alto, New York, and London.

items.title: It's great that OpenAI is doing these assessments but they fall short of Sam's commitment to employe...
items.content:
It's great that OpenAI is doing these assessments but they fall short of Sam's commitment to employee-like access

Good access is key for trust because assessors can find things even if a company tries hiding them. Here OpenAI controls information flow so we must rely on good faith

Limitations (per Apollo): 
- No Slack
- Only OpenAI-selected staff for interviews
- Formal conversations with staff must be logged (harder to freely raise concerns)
- METR & Apollo currently have only agreed access to training run information, not internal incidents, etc. Incidents like Hugging Face are some of the most important sources of information we have about alignment

I see the value in a pilot before future assessments with deeper access, but then OpenAI should present a plan for how and when they intend to meet their commitment to employee-like access. And either way, OpenAI is presumably able to go further here.

items.title:
The open-source LLM ecosystem could really benefit from an LLM building-block API.

We have so many ...
items.content:
The open-source LLM ecosystem could really benefit from an LLM building-block API.

We have so many LLM components across different models now. Whether you are using PyTorch or C++ and CUDA code directly, there is a major switching cost when you want to run experiments or ablation studies, say swapping GQA with MLA, dense FFNs with MoE, attention layers with Mamba2 or Gated DeltaNet, or standard residual connections with attention residuals.

Currently, it’s very messy even with LLM-assisted coding.

It could maybe be on top of PyTorch or CUDA directly, but it needs to be carefully engineered and maintained (versus quickly vibe-coded on a weekend) and efficient enough that people trust it to use in production (which is really a requirement to move beyond toy examples).

Maybe some food for thought for a big, well-funded lab :)

(There are some efforts that go into that direction, like torchtitan, torchtune, Megatron Core, OLMo-core, but they are not quite that level of abstraction, I'd say. 

And, as always, there’s the chicken-and-egg problem: it needs to be popular to get widely adopted, and it needs to get widely adopted to become popular.)

Announcing Artificial Analysis Time to First Audio, measuring how quickly Text to Speech models start speaking. Among the leading models the wait ranges from 76 ms to nearly a second

Our Text to Speech benchmarks already cover quality, pronunciation and generation speed, but not how long a user waits before hearing anything — the number that decides whether a voice agent feels responsive. We measure every model daily on the same 12 prompts across four input lengths, timing audible speech rather than the first byte, and report a rolling 7-day mean.

Key results:

➤ Fastest at the frontier: @SpeechifyAI's Simba 3.5 starts in 116 ms — the highest Arena Elo of any model that begins speaking in under 200 ms. @InworldAI's Realtime TTS-2 follows at 186 ms.

➤ Turbo variants earn their name: @ElevenLabs' Eleven v4 Turbo starts in 258 ms against 653 ms for Eleven v4, at the same Arena Elo. @FishAudio's Fish Audio Drama 3 matches it at 258 ms and @cartesia's Sonic 3.6 is at 287 ms.

➤ Streaming is the dividing line: The 65 streaming models typically begin speaking within a few hundred milliseconds, a median of 376 ms. The 20 non-streaming models must finish generating before they return anything: a median of 2.0 seconds.

See more details below ⬇️

items.content:
It's a joke but also not really a joke

Americans are really obsessed with work, and that's why they're so rich

But if there's no work to do anymore in a post-AGI world, everything becomes play

Who will be the best at play? At leisure life? Artistic pursuits? Social life?

It could actually be the Europeans because it's in their DNA to be exactly this

They're flâneurs (walking around without a goal), they sit in cafes for hours, have long lunches with friends, and are anything but productive yet feel great about it

items.title: Photon Health CEO @ottosipe reveals that doctors can now prescribe medication directly inside ChatGP...
items.content:
Photon Health CEO @ottosipe reveals that doctors can now prescribe medication directly inside ChatGPT for Clinicians.

Doctors can simply say, "Prescribe this to Patient X," and have the prescription texted to the patient seconds later:

"You can now actually prescribe in ChatGPT for Clinicians through Photon."

"Our claim to fame in some sense is enabling clinicians to text prescriptions to patients."

"What I think this really is a signal of is a shift toward agentic clinical workflows and agentic interfaces for patients."

"All you do is you say, 'Hey, prescribe this to Sophie,' and it'll go find Sophie's medical record and you get a text a few seconds later."

"It truly feels like magic."

"I got some chills on Friday morning when the first clinician used this in production."
@photonhealth

⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️  Wake the F up! ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️

items.content:
⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️  Wake the F up! ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️  

For months I have said, on practically every major TV network, “stop focusing on the doomers”

“Focus for now instead on the infrastructure and cybersecurity problems that agents are causing.”

“Recall general-purpose agents with internet access until the problems are solved. Require that new models have outside scientific review.”

But no. 

Instead people just played existential risk theatre, didn’t recall those agents. And attacked me relentlessly with propaganda and lies.

All we got was some voluntary “self-policing” at White House meeting. Which has done nothing.

So… Amtrak ground stop today, United Airlines issues today, Friday’s FAA ground stops (did we really get the full story on that?), banks today, French refrigeration incident a couple weeks ago, Open AI Hugging Face incident, Australian government hack, Binance and on and on, tens of thousands of incidents in the last few months.  

It can’t all be coincidence. Maybe not all of it is from AI agents but a lot of it probably is.

So yeah, quoting again @kasparov63, “I f_cking told you so.”

And we must take those agents off the market until the problems are resolved.

⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ Wake the F up! ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️ ⚠️

For months I have said, on practically every major TV network, “stop focusing on the doomers”

“Focus for now instead on the infrastructure and cybersecurity problems that agents are causing.”

“Recall general-purpose agents with internet access until the problems are solved. Require that new models have outside scientific review.”

But no.

Instead people just played existential risk theatre, didn’t recall those agents. And attacked me relentlessly with propaganda and lies.

All we got was some voluntary “self-policing” at White House meeting. Which has done nothing.

So… Amtrak ground stop today, United Airlines issues today, Friday’s FAA ground stops (did we really get the full story on that?), banks today, French refrigeration incident a couple weeks ago, Open AI Hugging Face incident, Australian government hack, Binance and on and on, tens of thousands of incidents in the last few months.

It can’t all be coincidence. Maybe not all of it is from AI agents but a lot of it probably is.

So yeah, quoting again @kasparov63, “I f_cking told you so.”

And we must take those agents off the market until the problems are resolved.

items.title:
Parsing forms is a hard problem, whether with specialized OCR or frontier models.

There is no stand...
items.content:
Parsing forms is a hard problem, whether with specialized OCR or frontier models.

There is no standardization across various form templates. There are multiple form elements (e.g. checkboxes, signatures, text fields) that need to be represented in various ways. A good parser needs to both extract empty/filled form values along with exact bounding boxes.

We’ve spent time carefully crafting a forms dataset within ParseBench-2. It consists of 600 pages from 244 government form templates across 30 countries, with 20K annotated fields (text, checkboxes, signatures).

We also designed a forms metric that’s weighted by severity policies, like the following:
- Blank fields have to stay blank
- Formatting changes cost nothing
- A lost signature counts 5
- A wrong number costs min 10

Different form extraction use cases will prioritize different errors more, and we encourage you to tune your own severity policies for form parsing.

More details in our blog / tech report: https://t.co/xtgxfln8Wc
Benchmark: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX
Available on Hugging Face! https://t.co/T1FLO2V2xd

items.title: I keep having the same conversation with friends in creative fields like film, music and publishing....
items.content:
I keep having the same conversation with friends in creative fields like film, music and publishing. I show them something a new model made and they say it’s good. But then they say AI will never tell a good story, because it lacks a certain je ne sais quoi.

I think my friends are wrong about one word: never.

Artists are already using AI to do remarkable work. I’m talking about something else here. I mean media made with little or no human involvement, where no person made the important choices. We have models that can generate a book, a film or a song this way. Most of what they make is not yet good enough for people to take seriously. The key word is “yet.”

Mathematicians had their own je ne sais quoi. They often talk about beauty, divergence, intuition and taste. Math as an art form. Then in September OpenAI announced that a swarm of about ten thousand agents had produced a proposed solution to  Navier-Stokes, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, in roughly 88 hours. Nothing about the process felt like our romantic picture of human discovery. A proof doesn’t care how it was found.

An obvious reply is that math is verifiable and art is not. Our inability to explain artistic judgment is mistaken for the evidence that machines cannot learn it.

Art does have a verifier. It’s the audience. Popularity is no guarantee of artistic quality. Popular media can be terrible and important art only ever be appreciated by a few people. But we can recognize when a piece of media becomes culturally relevant: people talk about it, argue about it, review it and copy it. This verifier is slow and noisy, and it can take years to return an answer. It is also already running at an enormous scale. Art is being judged, even if it’s not being objectively “measured.”

Here is my prediction. Art’s Navier-Stokes moment will come when a substantial, fully generated work - an album or book, or feature film becomes a cultural phenomenon, with no human making the important choices. I mean something that a lot of people will love before they even know how it was made, and will still love after they know. I think it will happen by 2027.

That’s the bad news, if you want to see it that way. I expect much of what we watch, read and listen to will eventually come out of models. The good news is that people will keep making art for the joy of the process and for what it means to them and other people. So much of what makes art matter is what happens between humans after it’s made: how we experience it together, talk about it, and give it shared meaning.

items.content:
Guild AI CEO @jevering shares findings from a new survey revealing major gaps in enterprise AI agent management:

- 96% confident in agent inventories; 67% report incidents
- Only 42% have dashboards; fewer than 40% have audit trails
- 60% suspect shadow agents; 35% require registration
- Very few have kill switches

Companies are deploying AI agents faster than they can govern them.
@GuildAI

items.content:
Here is a practical way to decide which model is the best for a job:

First, let me introduce the Specialized Intelligence Index (SII). This is a collection of tests and leaderboards to evaluate different models on domain-specific tasks.

You can find benchmarks across many domains, like reviewing contracts, answering customer questions, and writing code.

Here is something important:

These tests evaluate much more than whether a model produces a good result (which matters, but isn't enough).

The people who designed these tests understand the jobs. The tests evaluate what models need to accomplish, which constraints they must follow, and what makes the result acceptable.

If you want to know which model is the best at doing one specific job, you can use the SII to compare them across three parameters:

• Quality
• Cost
• Speed

You can find the benchmarks here: https://t.co/o8qOqZ9BS1

Pay attention to the setup behind each benchmark. The prompts and tools used during a test can affect the results.

Thanks to the @FireworksAI_HQ team for partnering with me on this post.

SITUATION EXPLAINED: Valar Atomics just won approval for up to 120 nuclear reactors in Utah, and the Senate advanced its biggest permitting overhaul in decades.

• Valar's Raceway Energy Campus would put 40 to 120 small reactors, a natural gas plant and data centers on 640 acres near Wellington, Utah
• Valar still needs NRC licenses before it can build any reactors there

• The 73-25 vote opened debate on the bill, which still needs a final Senate vote and then the House

items.title: Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making...
items.content:
Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later.

It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the photons as a pixel with a value of 0.5, so you can do the obvious linear math to calculate partial pixel coverage, blending a foreground over a background, or interpolating between colors in a texture.

If displays are “linear”, that is correct. NeXT and 3DFX were much closer to linear than other contemporary displays. NeXT had crossover from the deep graphics understanding at Pixar, and 3DFX had the SGI heritage. They did this intentionally.

If you have 10+ bits per channel like the professional rendering systems, linear displays are The Right Thing.

Unfortunately, NeXTStation Colors were 4 bits per channel and 3DFX was 5 or 6 bits per channel, and there… it was not the right thing.

Human eyes aren’t linear intensity sensors. We mostly register relative changes in intensity, so we can tell the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as a huge doubling, while 0.99 to 1.00 is almost imperceptible.

This distribution of intensities is often referred to as the “gamma” of the display system, but the actual curves like sRGB are a bit more complicated.

If you only have a small number of discrete pixel values, you definitely don’t want to spread them evenly from 0 to 1! If you do, you will have good precision in the brights, but very stark “intensity bands” in the dark colors.

If everything was authored specifically for 3DFX, you would still have the fundamental problem with the dark bands, but more accurate blending and filtering. The problem was that artists made all of their textures in paint programs on conventional non-linear displays, so when they were drawn by 3DFX cards, they got the characteristic “washed out color” look.

You can mathematically correct textures for differences in display gamma, but I didn’t really understand the issue back in the glQuake days, and we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have.

Even today, tons of games don’t properly handle gamma across their textures and render targets. High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges.
items.author: @ID_AA_Carmack
items.summary: John Carmack writes a detailed technical thread on color spaces: NeXT and 3DFX intentionally pursued linear display pipelines (influenced by Pixar and SGI heritage), which is correct with 10+ bits per channel but produced worse-looking results at 4-6 bits per channel because human vision is not linear. Strong engagement: ~4k likes and over 104k views.

items.summary_html: John Carmack writes a detailed technical thread on color spaces: NeXT and 3DFX intentionally pursued linear display pipelines (influenced by Pixar and SGI heritage), which is correct with 10+ bits per channel but produced worse-looking results at 4-6 bits per channel because human vision is not linear. Strong engagement: ~4k likes and over 104k views.
items.content_html:
Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later.

It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the photons as a pixel with a value of 0.5, so you can do the obvious linear math to calculate partial pixel coverage, blending a foreground over a background, or interpolating between colors in a texture.

If displays are “linear”, that is correct. NeXT and 3DFX were much closer to linear than other contemporary displays. NeXT had crossover from the deep graphics understanding at Pixar, and 3DFX had the SGI heritage. They did this intentionally.

If you have 10+ bits per channel like the professional rendering systems, linear displays are The Right Thing.

Unfortunately, NeXTStation Colors were 4 bits per channel and 3DFX was 5 or 6 bits per channel, and there… it was not the right thing.

Human eyes aren’t linear intensity sensors. We mostly register relative changes in intensity, so we can tell the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as a huge doubling, while 0.99 to 1.00 is almost imperceptible.

This distribution of intensities is often referred to as the “gamma” of the display system, but the actual curves like sRGB are a bit more complicated.

If you only have a small number of discrete pixel values, you definitely don’t want to spread them evenly from 0 to 1! If you do, you will have good precision in the brights, but very stark “intensity bands” in the dark colors.

If everything was authored specifically for 3DFX, you would still have the fundamental problem with the dark bands, but more accurate blending and filtering. The problem was that artists made all of their textures in paint programs on conventional non-linear displays, so when they were drawn by 3DFX cards, they got the characteristic “washed out color” look.

You can mathematically correct textures for differences in display gamma, but I didn’t really understand the issue back in the glQuake days, and we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have.

Even today, tons of games don’t properly handle gamma across their textures and render targets. High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges.

items.title: A free book Multivariate Statistical Machine Learning Methods for Genomic Prediction by Osval Antoni...
items.content:
A free book Multivariate Statistical Machine Learning Methods for Genomic Prediction by Osval Antonio Montesinos López, Abelardo Montesinos López, José Crossa.

The book’s focus is how to build, prepare, compare, and use prediction models for genomic selection. It begins with the training-population and testing-population framework, distinguishes prediction from inference, and introduces data types, learning paradigms, and fixed, random, and mixed effects.

It then connects those foundations to practical preparation of genomic data: marker cleaning, genomic relationship matrices, breeding-value estimation, normalization, predictor choices, and dimension reduction. 

he progression from multiple regression and penalized regression to mixed models, Bayesian methods, kernels, support vector machines, neural networks, functional regression, and random forests gives readers a broad view of model families and the assumptions and tasks they address.

Read the book online on @ChapterPal: https://t.co/4m0HBKwEff

items.title: Agents that work in open-ended environments must build skills over time, reuse them on new tasks, an...
items.content:
Agents that work in open-ended environments must build skills over time, reuse them on new tasks, and correct mistakes without losing dependable capabilities. Existing approaches often store skills as separate routines or static libraries, making it difficult to trace failures through multi-step behavior, improve the right components, and keep the library manageable. The article presents the Programmatic Skill Network (PSN), a framework designed to address these challenges by treating skills as executable programs linked into a network that can evolve with experience.

The article evaluates whether PSN can improve the acquisition, reliability, reuse, and organization of skills across unfamiliar and increasingly complex tasks. Its central idea is to combine three processes: analyze execution records to identify which parts of a skill sequence caused failure and propose targeted repairs; reduce updates to skills that have become reliable while continuing to improve less-tested ones; and reorganize the network to remove duplication and create reusable abstractions. Proposed structural changes are checked against recent performance and reversed if they cause a substantial decline. LLMs generate and diagnose code, but the framework supplies the learning and safeguards around them.

I...
items.content:
Reactorfield co-founders @berkbuilds and @jamessinka expected AI to automate scientific research.

Instead, their first cohort used it to discover new ways to produce isotopes:

"AI actually created net new science."

Berk: "When we first started our cohort one in June, our primary idea was to help scientists to use AI so that they can automate stuff. Literature search, writing, some boring stuff."

James: "One of our fellows actually compressed down a 25-minute workflow for data analysis down to 25 seconds. This is what we expected would happen."

Berk: "But what we ended up with, AI actually realized some pathways that we can produce some isotopes."
@ReactorfieldAI

items.title: The efficiency with which I now import books into ChapterPal and validate them is insane. I finally ...
items.content:
The efficiency with which I now import books into ChapterPal and validate them is insane. I finally automated the entire process.

I only submit the source URL, and the book is imported (from HTML, LaTeX, Markdown, ePub, and PDF), converted into ChaoterPal's Markdown flavor, and validated for high fidelity to the source. Chapter summaries, reading time, difficulty score, number of illustrations and exercises are computed; the book's executive summary and why-read sentence are generated; the authors and year are set; the license is checked; and the book is published.

I then only have to generate an aesthetically pleasing cover and post a link on X.

So, my role now is to find a good-quality book, submit the URL, and pick one cover image from several candidates.

I'm working on automating this part too, but I'm not sure whether the "aesthetically pleasing" part can be automated. We'll see.

ChapterPal will have nearly 600 high-quality online textbooks adapted for reading with an AI tutor in its collection by the end of the year.

Reactorfield co-founder @jamessinka explains why demand for AI intelligence in science is effectively unlimited:

You don't need a 1,000-IQ assistant for emails, but you need extreme intelligence to understand the Big Bang.

"Science is like an infinite game. There's no limit to the amount of new science we can discover, and so it's sort of the last and final frontier where our appetite and demand for tokens is unlimited."

"I think AI's on the trajectory to unlock that for society."
@ReactorfieldAI

"This is the drone that we built in six days to test the AI agent product that we’re making."

"We're Normal. We're an applied research company for people building things in the physical world, so hardware design and manufacturing."

"One of the things that we're building now is Zeus, which is an agent to act as your coworker and your tools to help you design hardware and help you source it and help you produce it."

"We said, 'What is the craziest thing that you can build in roughly the span of a week?' And they said, 'Let's build a Tesla Roadster. Let's build a boat.' And eventually we landed on a heavy lift drone."

items.title:
A free online book: Theory of Computing: An Open Introduction by Taylor J. Smith (2024).

It's an un...
items.content:
A free online book: Theory of Computing: An Open Introduction by Taylor J. Smith (2024).

It's an undergraduate-focused textbook on what computation can and cannot do.

The central organizing idea is a progression in computational power. Readers begin with regular expressions and finite automata, which recognize regular languages, then study context-free grammars and pushdown automata, whose stack allows them to describe and recognize a broader class of languages. Turing machines add tape-based memory and provide the framework for studying general computation.

At each stage, the book relates different representations of the same language or computation, develops constructions that translate between models, and identifies the limits that remain. These comparisons build toward a view of the Chomsky hierarchy and the distinctions among regular, context-free, decidable, and semidecidable languages.

It assumes familiarity with basic mathematical notation, while an appendix reviews sets, sequences, relations, functions, and graphs to support readers who want a refresher.

The book presents theory as a way to understand the capacities and limits of computation through precise abstract models, with examples that connect those models to familiar tools and computing situations.

Read the book online on @chapterpal: https://t.co/sIdQNNQXcM

items.title: Acorns CEO Noah Kerner says taxes are the biggest check Americans write over their lifetimes, yet th...
items.content:
Acorns CEO Noah Kerner says taxes are the biggest check Americans write over their lifetimes, yet they never get a receipt showing where the money goes.

His new startup Accountable plans to change that:

"Accountable started with a question 20 years ago, and the question was, why is it that taxpayers view taxes as a burden rather than an investment?"

"This is the largest check that we're ever gonna write across our lifetimes. It's actually really hard to write it. It's very hard to understand how it works, and then you don't even get a receipt or have any control over where the money goes."

"What Accountable is launching in January is gonna be a fast and fair way to file your taxes, and we're gonna launch the first taxpayer receipt. We're gonna show you at the federal, state, and local levels where your money actually goes."
@accountableusa

A free online book Godot Engine: Your first 2D game
by Juan Linietsky and Ariel Manzur (2026).

Godo...
items.content:
A free online book Godot Engine: Your first 2D game
by Juan Linietsky and Ariel Manzur (2026).

Godot Engine is a free, open-source, cross-platform game engine used to create both 2D and 3D games, as well as interactive applications and XR experiences. 

Godot Engine: Your first 2D game is a hands-on beginner’s book about building a complete, small 2D game in Godot. The tutorial follows the creation of “Dodge the Creeps!”, in which a player avoids incoming enemies and tries to survive as long as possible. It supports both GDScript and C#, with additional setup requirements for C#.

The book teaches Godot’s editor and project organization through one connected project. It begins with display settings and a scene structure that separates the player, enemies, and user interface into reusable components, then combines them in a main scene.

Along the way, readers learn how nodes and scenes divide responsibilities, how to add sprites, animations, and collision shapes, and how to attach scripts that control behavior.

Read the book online on @ChapterPal: https://t.co/wTqEhStIxK

For some reason, Google doesn't want to put AdSense ads on ChapterPal (though it puts these ads on really bad sites), so I'm looking for an alternative.

I want to show ads only to unauthenticated users and users on a free plan. This way, the ads will at least partially cover the hosting, compute, and AI costs for these users.

Any ideas are welcome.

items.title:
On the mathematics of being a book author.

When you see that a book in a bookstore is expensive, li...
items.content:
On the mathematics of being a book author.

When you see that a book in a bookstore is expensive, like $65, always remember that what the author usually gets is the amount in the bottom right corner of the screenshot below.

The authors are ripped off by the industry, and the industry isn't going to change.

This is also why you get a book from a major publisher that has gray paper of toilet-paper quality, with black-and-white illustrations, and falls apart when you read the first 20 pages.

They don't care whether the reader concludes that the author is a cheapskate and stop buying their books. The publisher has a waiting line of authors, especially today, when you can get a book in a single prompt.

This is why I don't work with publishers for my original English-language editions. Never did, even before slop.

I use the best paper and the best paint, and my books don't fall apart. The system rips me off, yes, but the readers are always happy with my books and can read and reread them many times and share them with friends.

@gregoryphopper I don't need a publisher to get books at home; I can get them from the printing company, but then I'll have a full-time job as a book wrapper and box taper. I love to write books, not to be a cashier.
